title: Mystic Treatises by Isaac of Nineveh
author: Isaac of Nineveh (Isaac the Syrian), 7th century
translator: A. J. Wensinck (from Bedjan's Syriac text)
edition_cited: Amsterdam: Koninklijke Akademie van Wetenschappen, Verhandelingen, Afd. Letterkunde, N.R. XXIII no. 1, 1923. archive.org item IsaacOfNinevehMysticTreatises
tradition: East Syrian Christian solitaries; read throughout the Orthodox hesychast tradition
locator_hints: Treatise XX 'On the revelations and powers which happen to the saints in images' (about lines 5640-5690; printed pp. 105-107): revelations through the bodily senses; Paul's light was 'no sensible light'

Treatise XXII 'On various experiences during prayer' (lines 5727-6095; printed pp. 108-118): 'delight during prayer is different from sight during prayer'; the mind seeing its own steadfastness 'resembling sapphire or the colour of heaven' (quoting Evagrius)
Search 'light of the mind', 'apperception', 'species' (lines 16220-16255 on affections as dense things between light and sight)
summary: A large body of ascetical treatises for solitaries. The relevant parts are Treatise XX, which classifies revelations (those through the bodily senses, those of the soul in images, those of the mind) and says that the light shown to Paul was 'no sensible light, but an incomprehensible apperception' given 'in the likeness of a vision of light'; and Treatise XXII on experiences during prayer, which separates delight from 'sight during prayer', and cites Evagrius on the mind seeing its own state at prayer 'resembling sapphire or the colour of heaven' over which the light of the Trinity rises. Isaac states he has experienced little of what he writes. The practice context is solitude, vigils, psalmody and stillness; nothing is offered as a technique for producing light.
why_relevant: Carries the Evagrian report of the mind's sapphire-coloured light at prayer and an early Eastern classification of sense-borne versus imaginal versus intellectual revelation, useful for the perceptual-versus-imaginal tag. Mostly doctrine; marginal on practice.
